questions.q: What is the rule for multiplying two fractions?
questions.a: To multiply two fractions, you multiply the numerators together to get the new numerator and the denominators together to get the new denominator. A wrong answer like "add the denominators" reveals a confusion between the rules for addition/subtraction and multiplication.

questions.q: If you multiply 1/2 by 1/4, will the result be larger or smaller than 1/2? Why?
questions.a: The result will be smaller (1/8) because you are taking a fraction of a fraction. Answering "larger" shows the student is incorrectly applying whole-number multiplication logic where products are always larger than factors.
(2 × 3) / (5 × 4) = 6/20. Simplified, this is 3/10. Answering 5/9 or 6/9 shows the student is attempting to cross-multiply or add instead of multiplying directly across.

questions.q: Compare the calculation 1/3 × 1/5 with the addition 1/3 + 1/5. Why are the results different?
questions.a: The product is 1/15, while the sum is 8/15. The results differ because multiplication finds a portion of a portion, while addition combines two distinct quantities, requiring different operational rules. Failing to see this distinction suggests the student views "fractions" as just numbers and not as parts of a whole.

questions.q: If a recipe requires 2/3 of a cup of milk, and you decide to make only 1/2 of the recipe, how much milk do you need? Justify your calculation.
questions.a: You need 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/6 = 1/3 cup of milk. The student must justify that taking half of two-thirds means multiplying them. Answering 2/3 shows a failure to recognize the need for multiplication in a "part of a part" scenario.

questions.q: Create a real-life word problem where you would need to multiply 3/4 by 1/2.
questions.a: A good answer would involve a physical quantity: "If you have 3/4 of a litre of juice and drink half of it, how much juice did you drink?" A poor answer would just be a string of numbers or an addition-based scenario, showing they haven't grasped that multiplication implies taking a fraction "of" a quantity.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Multiplying fractions is the process of finding a part of a part; it involves multiplying the numerators to form the new numerator and multiplying the ______ to form the new denominator.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have half a bar of ______ and you want to give one-third of that half to your friend.
What is Multiplying fractions? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Multiplying fractions is the process of finding a part of a part; it involves multiplying the numerators to form the new numerator and multiplying the denominators to form the new denominator.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Multiplying fractions?
questions.a: Students often try to find a common denominator before multiplying, just as they do with addition and subtraction.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to calculate the product of two fractions correctly and explain why the result is typically smaller than the original fractions when using proper fractions.
